description: We are a team of three Environmental Engineering students from Peru, passionate about sustainability, climate change, and environmental innovation. We aim to use NASA's open data to develop practical solutions to real-world environmental challenges. Our interests include water resources, environmental monitoring, and data analysis. We welcome collaboration with people skilled in programming, GIS, and satellite data analysis.
summary:
HydroTrends is a reproducible rainfall-trend analysis tool developed by Team SPIN to investigate how precipitation patterns are represented across Peruvian river basins.

We combined NASA GPM IMERG V07 and SENAMHI PISCOp data to analyze rainfall in Huancapata/Ambo, Piura, and Santa. Our workflow processes monthly precipitation, estimates seasonal trends using the Theil–Sen method, and performs quality checks. We also developed an interactive desktop viewer where users can explore basins, compare datasets, examine scientific limitations, and download reproducible CSV and JSON results.

HydroTrends addresses the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge by investigating an important finding: different rainfall products can suggest opposite trends for the same basin. Rather than presenting uncertain conclusions as facts, our tool makes these disagreements visible and clearly identifies results requiring further investigation.

This matters because understanding environmental change requires more than producing graphs. By making evidence transparent, traceable, and accessible, HydroTrends supports scientific learning, responsible interpretation, and better-informed environmental research.
details:
HydroTrends SPIN — Project Details

HydroTrends SPIN is a reproducible Earth observation and data visualization tool designed to investigate precipitation trends across Peruvian watersheds. Our project addresses NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” by transforming satellite observations into accessible, traceable, and scientifically interpretable information.

How does it work?

HydroTrends processes monthly precipitation data from NASA’s GPM IMERG V07 satellite product and compares them with SENAMHI’s PISCOp precipitation dataset. Our initial study covers three Peruvian watersheds: Upper Huallaga (Huancapata-Ambo), Piura, and Santa.

The system processes monthly observations from 2001-2024 and evaluates seasonal patterns, including 23 complete December-February seasons from 2002–2024. It applies basin-weighted spatial aggregation, data quality checks, Theil-Sen trend estimation, Mann-Kendall testing, autocorrelation adjustments, and uncertainty assessments.

Results are presented through a visual interface that helps users explore precipitation patterns, examine methodological limitations, and download supporting CSV and JSON files.

What makes our project innovative?

HydroTrends does more than display climate data: it makes scientific uncertainty visible.

Different precipitation datasets can produce conflicting trends for the same watershed. Instead of concealing these differences or automatically declaring a climate trend, HydroTrends identifies disagreements and distinguishes descriptive evidence from conclusions that require further validation.

This approach combines transparent statistical analysis, reproducible processing, geographic visualization, and accessible communication.

Technologies and development

Our workflow combines Python for data processing and statistical analysis; JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interactive viewer; Google Earth Engine for geospatial and satellite-data workflows; and GIS-based watershed geometries. CSV, JSON, and GeoJSON support data exchange, traceability, and reproducibility.

The project is software-based and does not require specialized hardware to explore its prepared results.

Benefits and intended impact

HydroTrends aims to make Earth observation data more understandable and useful to students, researchers, environmental professionals, and communities interested in water resources.

By focusing on Peruvian watersheds, we connect global satellite observations with local environmental questions while encouraging responsible interpretation of scientific evidence.

Our long-term vision is to extend the workflow toward independently reproducible analyses for additional watersheds.

Ultimately, HydroTrends demonstrates that meaningful Earth system investigation requires more than detecting a trend: it requires understanding the evidence, its uncertainty, and the limits of what the data can tell us.
